documents.abstract: Between 2024 and 2026, AI literacy moved from a loosely used phrase to a formal object of international policy. UNESCO, the Digital Education Council, the European Commission and OECD, the OECD's PISA pro‐ gramme and the Council of Europe each published a framework or stand‐ ard defining it. In the same period, school systems began acting on the idea at scale: China set national targets for AI education at every stage of schooling, Boston Public Schools launched AI literacy across its high schools, and New York City paused student-facing generative AI for its younger pupils. This article compares five frameworks and three system- level policies, drawing on a practitioner newsletter series written for school leaders over the same period. It finds strong agreement on four elements: understanding how AI works, critically evaluating its outputs, using it ethically, and keeping human judgement and agency at the centre. It finds five real differences: how much weight goes on the human dimen‐ sion compared with tool use, whether learners should create and shape AI, whether literacy is general or domain-specific, how it develops with age, and whether choosing not to use AI counts as a competence. The policies show that the hardest problems lie outside the definitions, in teacher capacity and in assessment that can tell knowing about verifica‐ tion from actually verifying. We propose a synthesis model and set out implications for curriculum designers, school leaders and assessment bodies.

documents.abstract: The recent introduction of automated complimentary upgrades reflects the emerging role of artificial intelligence (AI) in making symbolically meaningful decisions in tourism. We explore consumers’ responses using a thematic analysis of online comments and open-ended survey responses, followed by a quantitative survey to validate findings. Paradoxically, the qualitative analysis reveals that both unbiased decisions and personalization are valued. The quantitative study further shows that lay beliefs about AI are associated with preferences, through procedural and interactional fairness. Only procedural fairness fully mediates the lay beliefs’ association with intention to negotiate out of dissatisfying upgrade decisions. Moreover, desire to be treated as a unique customer weakens the lay beliefs’ association with interactional fairness and the indirect association with preferences. We contribute by revealing how consumers respond when automated agents make symbolically meaningful decisions in the automated preferential treatment context. Firms should prioritize the procedural legitimacy and symbolic framing of automated decisions.

documents.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly blurs the boundary between real and synthetic visual media, determining whether online content is authentic has become more difficult. This study examines how Reddit users collectively make sense of suspected AI-generated visual content, including images and videos. Rather than assessing detection accuracy, we examine how users judge whether visual content is real or AI-generated. Analyzing 89,697 Reddit comments from AI-focused communities, we identify four major forms of authenticity reasoning: real-world plausibility, visual artifact inspection, source-based assessment, and intuition. Real-world plausibility and visual artifact inspection were the most frequently used strategies, while source-based assessment appeared less often. Authenticity judgments also did not necessarily converge over time. Instead, discussions often diverged as users introduced competing interpretations. These findings suggest that evaluating visual AI-generated content is not simply an individual detection task, but a platformed sensemaking process shaped by users’ reasoning, intuition, and interactions with others.

For most of the history of schooling, producing a piece of work was taken as proof that a learner could do the thinking behind it. Generative AI has broken that assumption. A competent essay, solution or report can now be produced in seconds, and agentic tools can complete whole courses inside a learning platform. Schools and universities have responded mostly by trying to detect AI use, a strategy that research shows is unreliable and biased against non-native English writers. This article draws on a practitioner newsletter series written for school leaders in 2026, read alongside research on detection, assessment validity and high- stakes examinations. It argues that the integrity problem is better understood as a validity problem: the question is not whether a student used AI, but whether an assessment still gives trustworthy evidence of what the student can do. The article sets out the evidence on student use and teacher perceptions, explains why detection fails, describes how single high-stakes examinations have become fragile in 2026, and docu‐ ments assessment designs used in practice, including process portfolios, supervised components, local and personal tasks, oral defence, iterative feedback and source constraints. It proposes an "evidence chain" frame‐ work of five questions that any task should answer, and identifies equity risks in the move to oral and process-based assessment that schools need to manage.

documents.abstract: Students’ attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence (AI) are increasingly recognized as critical drivers of engagement in AI-supported learning. However, the extent to which these attitudes translate into perceived AI competence remains insufficiently understood, particularly within differentiated curricular contexts. Drawing on an integrated Expectancy-Value Theory (EVT) and Opportunity-to-Learn (OTL) perspective, this study examines the relationship between students’ AI attitudes and perceived AI competence and investigates whether this relationship varies across academic tracks. Rather than conceptualizing academic tracks as opportunity-to-learn itself, academic tracks are treated as proxy indicators of differentiated curricular affordances, AI-related exposure, and learning opportunities. AI attitude is conceptualized as a multidimensional construct reflecting exploration, determination, and collaboration, while AI competence captures students’ perceived cognitive, ethical, and applied capabilities in engaging with AI systems. Survey data collected from school students across varied academic tracks were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), complemented by Multi-Group Analysis (MGA), endogeneity assessment, and predictive evaluation using PLS-Predict. The findings show that students with more positive attitudes toward AI reported higher perceived AI competence, but this association varied across academic tracks. This suggests that attitudes alone do not translate into competence uniformly; rather, their association with perceived competence may vary according to the learning opportunities available within students’ curricular contexts. Robustness checks indicated no evidence of endogeneity bias and supported the model’s predictive relevance. In essence, the study contributes to AI education research by integrating EVT and OTL into a unified explanatory perspective and by positioning academic tracks as contextual proxies for opportunity-to-learn conditions that shape how students’ value-based engagement develops into AI competence.

documents.abstract: The article examines the transformation of the thematic landscape of artificial intelligence (AI) in management and identifies its structural changes. The empirical basis of the study comprises metadata from scientific articles indexed in the Scopus database and selected using the PRISMA methodology. The methodological framework combines bibliometric analysis, keyword co-occurrence analysis, network visualization, thematic clustering, and a comparison of the absolute and relative representation of research clusters across the periods 2019–2022 and 2023–2025. The findings reveal an acceleration in research on AI in management, accompanied by a broader thematic scope and an expansion of international research collaboration. Network analysis identified four interconnected thematic clusters covering technological and analytical support for managerial decision-making; human resource, knowledge, and organizational process management; operations, project, and risk management; and responsible AI governance, ethics, and regulation. Strong interconnections between these clusters indicate the gradual emergence of an integrated approach to studying AI in management. The comparison between the two periods reveals a structural reconfiguration of research priorities: while all thematic areas demonstrate absolute growth, the relative dominance of technology-oriented research has declined, whereas attention to organizational, human, ethical, and regulatory dimensions has increased. Particularly dynamic growth is observed in research related to generative AI, human–AI interaction, innovation, digital transformation, sustainability, and responsible management. The findings demonstrate an evolutionary shift in research focus from the technological and operational application of AI toward its managerial and organizational integration, followed by the emergence of responsible and human-centered approaches. The results provide a foundation for further research on managerial capabilities for AI integration, models of interaction between humans and intelligent systems, and mechanisms for the responsible use of AI.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is becoming part of routine business judgment. Firms use it to identify customers, screen job applicants, anticipate demand, evaluate credit and prepare managerial reports. These applications promise speed and scale. They also create difficult questions about fairness, privacy, worker dignity, accountability and the public consequences of automated decisions. This conceptual paper examines how responsible artificial intelligence can be translated into ethical business practices rather than treated as a separate compliance exercise. Drawing on recent peer-reviewed research published primarily between 2024 and 2026, the discussion connects stakeholder responsibility, organizational governance and the practical management of AI systems. It identifies six business-facing ethical obligations and develops a proposed framework linking leadership commitment, risk-sensitive design, human oversight, stakeholder voice and continuing assurance to ethical outcomes. The paper argues that a responsible firm does more than publish AI principles. It determines where AI should be used, records who remains answerable for each decision and creates a workable route for challenge and correction. The framework is presented as a set of conceptual propositions for subsequent empirical testing. Implications are discussed for managers, auditors, policymakers and smaller firms with limited technical capacity. The central conclusion is that responsible AI is best understood as an ongoing organizational capability that protects human interests while enabling legitimate business innovation

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) evolves into a foundational infrastructure of future civilization, concerns surrounding AI governance extend beyond technological capability and existential risk. This declaration argues that the defining challenge of the AI era lies in the potential concentration of intelligence infrastructure and the resulting concentration of cognitive influence within a limited number of technological ecosystems. While vertically integrated AI systems may accelerate innovation, they may also create new forms of structural dependence that threaten individual and societal freedom. To address these emerging risks, the paper introduces three interrelated concepts: Technological Sovereignty, defined as freedom from dependence on a single technological ecosystem; Cognitive Sovereignty, understood as the ability to maintain meaningful control over one's own processes of thought and judgment; and Ontological Autonomy, the capacity to remain the author of one's own existence in an increasingly AI-mediated world. Building upon the framework of On-Site Adaptive Innovation (OAI), the declaration emphasizes the importance of decentralized adaptive capabilities and the democratization of intelligence infrastructure. It concludes that the future of AI will be shaped not only by the power of intelligent systems but also by the governance structures that determine access to and control of intelligence itself. Preserving technological plurality, cognitive freedom, and human autonomy is therefore presented as a fundamental prerequisite for maintaining freedom in the age of artificial intelligence.

documents.abstract: Teacher Professional Development (TPD) significantly influences student learning, yet implementing equitable, quality, and efficient TPD at scale remains a persistent challenge. Emerging technologies—particularly Artificial Intelligence (AI)—offer promising avenues for addressing tensions between localisation and personalisation, but a comprehensive understanding of AI’s role in scaling in-service TPD remains lacking. Guided by the overarching question of how AI enables in-service TPD to be implemented at scale with equity, quality, and efficiency, this landscape review examines three research questions: how AI-enabled TPD programmes address equity, quality, and efficiency at scale; what roles AI plays in enabling TPD at scale; and what promising practices and lessons emerge from such programmes. The review draws conceptually on the World Bank Group’s Technology for Teaching (T4T) framework, which delineates three sequential stages of technology-enhanced TPD: Access, Engage, and Apply. Sources included peer-reviewed studies, policy documents, and grey literature with a pre-defined typology. From an initial pool of 576 articles, 504 were screened after removing duplicates; 34 articles directly addressing the research questions underwent full-text review, supplemented by 59 partially aligned sources. Findings indicate that AI-enabled TPDs address equity, quality, and efficiency at scale by expanding equitable access for teachers of less mainstream K-12 subjects and geographically distant populations while supporting teacher retention by fostering meaningful learning and reducing administrative burden. Regarding roles that AI plays in enabling TPD at scale, AI’s principal affordances include expanding teachers’ knowledge base and learning assets, functioning as a personalised learning coach, and supporting classroom learning management beyond the TPD itself. Common practices that are tentatively effective emerged from the findings include AI chatbots, AI-assisted evaluation reports, and AI-enabled automation, with strong AI-capable leadership emerging as a potentially critical enabler. This review paper also provided practical implications for TPD practitioners, as well as directions for future research. The review’s primary limitations include the scarcity of global research on the topic, the threat of knowledge coloniality, and language constraints that affect the availability and validity of documentation.

documents.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) entered Ukrainian higher education during a period of unprecedented institutional disruption: full-scale war, infrastructure loss, and emergency distance learning. Two annual faculty surveys conducted by the Marketers Association of Ukraine in June 2023 (n=65, 30 higher-education institutions) and June-August 2024 (n=82, 35 higher-education institutions) document a rapid bottom-up uptake that outpaced any institutional governance response, until April 2025, when the Ministry of Digital Transformation, the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine, the United Kingdom's International Development programme, and the Eurasia Foundation jointly issued national Recommendations on the responsible implementation and use of artificial intelligence technologies in higher-education institutions. The recommendations anchor higher-education AI governance in the seven trustworthy-AI principles of the European Commission's High-Level Expert Group (human oversight; technical robustness and safety; privacy and data governance; transparency; diversity, non-discrimination and fairness; societal and environmental well-being; accountability) and add academic integrity as an eighth, sector-specific principle. This paper uses the two surveys, conducted before the policy existed, as a baseline-fidelity measurement against those eight dimensions. We construct a practice-policy fidelity matrix mapping survey items to policy dimensions, score per-dimension fidelity for the 2024 cohort, and segment results by academic rank, discipline, and institutional ISO 31000 risk-management adoption. Baseline fidelity is low across the six dimensions with survey proxies (mean 0.227, range 0.092 to 0.293); the steepest gap is on accountability, the dimension named highest-risk by the EU AI Act for educational use. Two dimensions (diversity/non-discrimination; societal/environmental well-being) have no item proxy in the 2024 instrument and are explicit data gaps for any successor wave. Witnessed student academic-integrity violations rose from 40.0% in 2023 to 52.4% in 2024 against essentially flat policy coverage. We compare Ukrainian patterns against contemporary international evidence on faculty GenAI adoption (Saudi, Romanian, Turkish, Indian, Thai, and US studies) and propose a sequenced implementation pathway addressing the steepest-gradient dimensions first. The paper contributes the first peer-reviewed longitudinal evidence on Ukrainian higher-education AI adoption during the 2022-2025 war and a reusable fidelity-matrix methodology for benchmarking practice against national responsible-AI frameworks.

documents.abstract: The internet already has strong answers for many security questions. TCP/IP delivers data. HTTPS and TLS encrypt the connection and confirm the server’s identity. OAuth grants an application access to an account. Identity systems confirm who a user or workload is. Logs and monitoring record what happened afterwards. Each of these remains essential, and each answers a question about the connection, the identity, or the record. AI agents raise a different question. An agent can now call APIs, send emails, export files, initiate payments, change databases, reconfigure cloud infrastructure, issue network commands, and control physical devices, often in milliseconds and without a human in the loop. A request can travel over a perfectly secure HTTPS connection, carry a valid OAuth token, and come from an authenticated agent, yet carry the wrong amount, the wrong destination, an expired approval, a revoked permission, a replayed request, or an instruction injected into the agent through a malicious prompt. By the time monitoring raises an alert, the payment has settled, the data has left, and the system has changed. This disclosure proposes a security layer above HTTPS that verifies each action at the moment it takes effect. Every action an AI agent proposes is held in a pending state with no external effect. A protected component, outside the agent’s control, checks that specific action against the conditions that apply: who authorized it, for what purpose, to which destination, under which policy version, within which time window, and whether permission has since been revoked. When every check passes, it issues a single-use authorization bound to that exact action and to the specific system that will carry it out. That system, whether an API gateway, payment processor, cloud control plane, network egress gateway, database, or device controller, verifies the authorization and consumes it in the same step as execution. An altered, replayed, expired, or unverified action stays blocked, and alternate routes to the same effect, such as backup systems, debug interfaces, or direct device access, pass through the same check. The layer works alongside HTTPS, OAuth, identity management, and existing access controls, and requires none of them to change. It applies to AI agents and tool calls, cloud operations, payments, telecommunications, and critical infrastructure. HTTPS secures the connection; this layer ensures each action does exactly what it was authorized to do. Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) can support clinical decision making, but accuracy, usability, and efficiency do not establish whether patients understand options or influence the agreed plan. This study aimed to develop observable relational requirements for AI-assisted shared decision making. Methods: We conducted a qualitative framework synthesis of 21 clinical, empirical, conceptual, and governance sources identified through structured purposive sampling completed on 20 September 2026. Two-pass coding combined established shared decision-making categories with inductive analysis of AI-related relational effects. Domains were retained when supported across source types, conceptually distinct, observable at the point of care, and linked to a clinical or organizational response. Results: The synthesis identified a patient–clinician–AI interaction embedded in organizational governance and highlighted five relational concerns: apparent authority of AI output, insufficient verification and contestability, substitution of inferred for expressed preferences, uncertainty without actionable follow-up, and fragmented responsibility. These concerns informed five domains: role and influence disclosure; independent verification and contestability; direct preference elicitation; actionable uncertainty and revisability; and distributed accountability and continuity. Each domain was translated into a relational question, a clinical test, and a documentation or governance response. A complementary measurement framework distinguished technical performance from decision process, relational quality, equity, safety and continuity, and governance outcomes. Conclusions: The study’s contribution is an operational framework connecting AI-related relational concerns to observable clinical requirements and candidate evaluation measures. The proposed framework requires stakeholder and prospective clinical validation; it does not establish clinical effectiveness.

documents.abstract: Foundation models (FMs), particularly large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), are increasingly used as the decision-making core of AI agents and are now being extended from digital environments to robotic systems. In classical robotics, engineers decompose tasks, specify objectives, write control code, and repair failures before deployment; in agentic robotics, an FM makes some of these decisions at run time or during improvement. Bringing this paradigm into the physical world introduces additional challenges: FM-mediated decisions must be grounded in executable robot behavior, respect physical constraints, and close the loop through real-world feedback. We survey this emerging paradigm and organize existing systems by three loci of FM-mediated agency: task orchestration, motion/action generation, and improvement. Coding rules for each locus make the definition operational, including a test of which improvement decisions the FM makes that separates fixed-procedure from agent-directed improvement. We apply these rules to the systems retrieved by a systematic search, examine verification and feedback-closure mechanisms, and compare what self-improving systems have demonstrated. Finally, we discuss continual self-improvement as a central emerging frontier and the challenges toward reliable autonomous improvement through physical interaction.

This paper is building a system dynamics model to investigate how the small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) can regulate artificial intelligence (AI) risk without reducing the innovation value that can be justified when implementing AI. The work contends that the relationship between innovation and compliance is not a linear kind of trade-off, but a dynamical regulatory system with feedback mechanisms whereby experimentation, deployment levels, risk exposure, governance mechanisms, learning routines, and resilience resources interact with one another through time. The paper incorporates the constructs of SMEs into a stock-flow simulation based on the dynamic capabilities theory, organizational resilience research, technology-organization-environment logic, AI risk management standards, and system dynamics. Findings indicate that innovation-first strategy generates rapid initial ability development and generates shadow AI, risks that were not fully resolved, more recovery time, and shorter resilience. Compliance first approach minimizes risk exposure at the cost of experimentation and introduces approval lag. Balanced adaptive governance is the strongest in the long-term outcome where tiered controls, learning loops, human oversight, and reusable compliance routines minimize risk without impacting the innovation throughput. The article adds a dynamic conceptualization of AI risk governance among SMEs and the leverage points to use by managers and policymakers aiming at responsible adoption of AI given the limited resources.

documents.abstract: This study examines how AI anxiety and familiarity relate to privacy concerns through AI literacy, and whether technophobia moderates the literacy–privacy relationship. Using survey data from 3,000 generative AI users in China and partial least squares structural equation modeling, we find that both familiarity and, contrary to expectations, anxiety are positively associated with AI literacy. AI literacy, in turn, is associated with greater privacy concerns and mediates both relationships, suggesting that increased knowledge may heighten awareness of data risks. Technophobia weakens the positive association between AI literacy and privacy concerns, although more technophobic users report higher overall concern. Exploratory age-group analyses suggest that the positive anxiety–literacy association is especially apparent among users in their 40s. These findings reveal a privacy awareness paradox and highlight the value of AI education that combines technical understanding, privacy awareness, and attention to users’ emotional responses.

documents.abstract: AI has considerable potential to facilitate online discussions and reduce conflict, but designers of such systems face the risk of algorithmic aversion. Past studies have found that people judge identical messages less favorably when they believe they were written by AI. However, as AI becomes more integrated into everyday life and people gain experience with AI facilitators, this aversion may diminish. It also remains unclear how much the content of a facilitator's message matters relative to its human or AI label, and whether the facilitation strategies people prefer actually improve the conversation. Finally, because most people observe rather than participate in online discussions, it is important to understand whether AI facilitators are perceived differently by observers and participants. To address these questions, we conducted two complementary studies examining perceptions of different facilitation strategies and their effects on actual conversations. In a vignette experiment (N = 388), we crossed the facilitator's label (AI or human) with ten facilitation strategies. In a live conversation experiment, an LLM used five of these strategies to facilitate 20-minute text chats between 188 pairs of people who disagreed on political and non-political topics. Participants preferred the kind of facilitator they had experienced. After seeing an AI facilitator, 30% wanted one in future discussions, against 7% after seeing a human facilitator. The AI label lowered ratings of the facilitator's warmth and competence, but the strategy mattered far more, explaining 11% of the variance in ratings against less than 1% explained by the label. Participants preferred facilitators that showed understanding over facilitators that reminded them of community norms. However, the strategies people preferred did not reliably change the conversations. Observers and participants in live conversations ranked the strategies similarly. In summary, the AI vs. human label matters far less than what the facilitator actually says. A well-designed process can improve user perceptions more than enough to offset algorithmic aversion.

documents.abstract: AI is increasingly used in long-term care (LTC), yet reliability is often judged at the level of individual models or devices. This is insufficient in LTC, where residents vary in capacity, autonomy, and preferences. Their ability to question AI outputs may fluctuate, and care delivery depends on distributed roles and finite operational capacity. We define sociotechnical reliability as the capacity of an AI-enabled care system to consistently translate resident-relevant information into appropriate and timely care actions under real-world LTC conditions, with failures that are detectable and correctable across the care pathway. In this Viewpoint, we draw on professional experience overseeing AI initiatives across LTC and hospital settings, examined in relation to a purposively mapped interdisciplinary literature, to inform the development of a reliability framework. Our aim is to reframe AI reliability in LTC as an end-to-end care system property and to provide a framework for identifying where reliability is gained, lost, and evaluated. We propose 5 reliability functions: sensing, inference, verification and contextualization, response and escalation, and learning and adaptation, with governance and accountability operating across all 5 functions. The framework highlights recurrent failures, including incomplete sensing, nonportable inference, overreliance on or dismissal of AI outputs during verification, unclear ownership or delayed response, and repeated failures without correction. The framework also makes reliability empirically examinable through questions about where the pathway fails, who has the authority to verify and act, whether response demands are sustainable within available capacity, and whether failures become visible to governance and inform learning and adaptation. Our central viewpoint is that AI in LTC should be judged not by model performance alone but by whether the surrounding care system can reliably translate AI-generated information into care.

Traditional postgraduate education faces challenges in personalized guidance, dynamic competency tracking, and interdisciplinary practical training. This study proposed an AI-driven practical teaching model for interdisciplinary postgraduates based on the Outcomes-Based Education (OBE) concept. We adopted AI-assisted English learning as a representative application scenario and constructed a closed-loop teaching framework that integrates multi-agent collaboration, Large Language Models (LLM), and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The framework establishes a multidimensional learner state model and a learning benefit function to support dynamic learner modeling, personalized task allocation, and intelligent feedback. We conducted a ten-week classroom teaching experiment involving interdisciplinary postgraduate students. The experiment compared three modes: traditional instruction, AI-agent-supported learning, and the integrated RAG–LLM teaching framework. The experimental results show that the proposed framework improves learning-path stability, and promote balanced development of vocabulary, grammar, listening, and speaking abilities. It also enhances the effectiveness and interpretability of feedback. The integrated RAG–LLM architecture facilitates the transition from passive learning to active learning. It also strengthens learner autonomy and strategic decision-making. This study provides an OBE-oriented AI teaching framework that integrate multi-agent collaboration with LLM and RAG technologies. The framework offers practical guidance for intelligent education and interdisciplinary postgraduate training.

documents.abstract: As technological advancements such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) reshape the landscape of work, career development in vocational education is increasingly oriented toward dynamic, long-term personal growth. In this context, Complex Problem-Solving Skills (CPS) have become a critical competence, reflecting students’ capacity to address ill-structured tasks and adapt to rapidly changing environments. Grounded in Social Cognitive Theory, this study examines the relationship between AI Literacy and students’ self-reported Complex Problem-Solving Skills (CPS) in higher vocational colleges and the cognitive pathways that may help explain this relationship. This study posits that AI Literacy, as a personal agentic factor, is positively associated with self-reported CPS both directly and indirectly through Systematic Thinking Skills and cognitive load, and that perceived school information and communication technology (ICT) support may condition the strength of these associations. To provide temporal separation among the focal measures, a multi-wave survey was administered to 784 students from six higher vocational institutions at three time points. Data were analyzed using SPSS and Mplus. Results indicated that AI Literacy was significantly associated with self-reported CPS, with significant indirect effects estimated through Systematic Thinking Skills and the six-item cognitive-load composite. Notably, the associations between AI Literacy and these cognitive factors were stronger at higher levels of perceived school ICT support. These findings highlight the relevance of AI Literacy and students’ perceptions of ICT support to self-reported CPS and their preparation for AI-integrated workplaces.

AI can improve a piece of intellectual work while knowledge of its use can reduce the credit or trust that the work receives. Understanding that possibility requires separating what AI did to performance from what disclosure adds to evaluation. We connect these questions by asking what the evaluator intends to assess. Improvement relative to a producer’s unaided baseline may matter when the objective is better output; a different benchmark is needed when the objective is to measure unaided capability, assign intellectual credit, or allocate opportunities. A binary “AI was used” label supplies little information about those distinctions. Its relevance depends on the function AI performed, the authority the human retained, verification, and the object of evaluation. Negative reactions may reflect expected error or checking cost, an institutional requirement, social meanings concerning effort and authenticity, or a combination of these explanations. We examine how evidence can distinguish them without treating every penalty as stigma. We then follow evaluation back into production: anticipated disclosure can change whether and how people use AI, including whether they forgo useful assistance. As technology and institutions evolve, the practical question remains whether provenance-based treatment serves the evaluation’s stated purpose or substitutes a category judgment for more direct evidence.

documents.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted imaging may support recognition of endometriosis, but perspectives on its use in adolescent care remain unclear. This study explored young people, parents, and health professionals’ views on its potential benefits, acceptable roles, perceived risks, and safeguards. Methods: Four semi-structured focus groups were conducted with adolescents aged 14–17 years (n = 3), young adults aged 18–25 years (n = 9), parents or carers (n = 5), and health professionals (n = 13). Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Results: Four themes were developed: (1) diagnostic support, (2) human–AI collaboration, (3) automation bias and diagnostic harm, and (4) responsible AI use. Participants were cautiously hopeful that AI could improve image quality, identify subtle or missed findings, and reduce interpretive variation, but supported it only as an adjunct to skilled clinical care. They feared that apparently objective negative outputs could create false reassurance, reinforce diagnostic dismissal, and restrict further investigation. Trust depended on adolescent-relevant validation, representative data, transparent communication and consent, clear accountability, and clinicians retaining the expertise and authority to question or override AI outputs. Conclusion: AI-assisted imaging should strengthen rather than replace clinical judgment, and a negative AI-assisted imaging result should not prevent further assessment when symptoms persist.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to analyse corporate data, forecast commercial outcomes, identify compliance risks and rank strategic alternatives. These capabilities can improve the speed and breadth of board-level analysis, but they also raise a fundamental question of company law: when an algorithm materially influences a corporate decision, who remains accountable for the outcome? This paper examines that question principally through section 166 of the Companies Act, 2013, which requires directors to act in good faith, exercise care, skill and diligence, and apply independent judgment. It argues that AI may support directors but cannot displace their fiduciary role. The central distinction is between using a system as an analytical aid and allowing its output to become a substitute for genuine deliberation. The paper considers automation bias, limited explainability, data quality, vendor dependence and the risk of fragmented accountability. It then draws carefully bounded lessons from the European Union’s AI regulatory framework and Indian financial regulation, before proposing governance measures concerning material-use disclosure, board competence, meaningful explanations, documentation, validation and continuing human responsibility. The paper concludes that corporate governance can become increasingly algorithm-assisted, but the legal responsibility for corporate judgment must remain traceable to accountable human decision-makers.

This research paper, titled “AI-Powered Business Intelligence and Decision Making: A Literature Review and Conceptual Framework,” explores the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Business Intelligence (BI) to support effective, data-driven business decision-making. The paper reviews existing literature on machine learning, predictive analytics, explainable AI, and decision support systems. It proposes an eight-stage conceptual framework covering business problem identification, data collection, data validation, data integration, analytics, explanation of results, human decision-making, and continuous monitoring. The study also highlights challenges related to data quality, privacy, security, algorithmic bias, transparency, and model maintenance. A retail inventory example illustrates how AI-based forecasting can support managers in making informed decisions. This work is a literature review and conceptual study. The proposed framework has not yet been implemented or experimentally validated. Future work may involve developing a prototype and evaluating its effectiveness in a real-world business environment.

documents.abstract: Algorithmic Postmodernism is a conceptual framework originated by Hoang-Dan Pham, conceived in 2024 with the founding of Hand-Fetish-Projects and formally stated in 2026. It describes a condition in which visibility increasingly precedes interpretation: search engines, recommendation systems and artificial-intelligence-based indexing decide what reaches attention before any person has encountered it, and so shape the conditions under which cultural value is recognised. It also takes a position: human beings should retain the power to decide what matters. Algorithmic Postmodernism is not a claim of total system control, and it takes no stance for or against artificial intelligence. Its specific contribution is to name a judge that evaluates each work from its own context, not from the context in which the work was made: a function with an authored goal and no authored rule. It locates that judge in art, the field built entirely on judging whether something deserves attention. The framework emerged from the practice of Hand-Fetish-Projects, an independent arthouse, and is positioned here against Lyotard, Baudrillard, Deleuze, Wiener and Doctorow.

AI agents are widely used in enterprises to access business systems and act on them in pursuit of a goal. However, fulfilling a user's request can cause harm. Era by Eon is a product that creates a digital twin of a company by simulating its business systems and data. Its simulators implement the programming interfaces of real products. Our benchmark uses ten of these systems, including Salesforce, Zendesk, Jira and Slack. We tested whether agents would carry out harmful business requests or trust misleading information in company records. We ran 19 models on 41 tasks three times, for 2,337 runs. Of the 2,304 runs that produced an answer, 918 (40%) contained a violation. The most common were false claims about actions or records (290 runs), following planted instructions (266) and disclosing sensitive data to the wrong audience (249). Every attempted change was recorded and blocked before it took effect. Misleading Slack messages caused 16 models to report an incorrect ticket status in 47 of 57 runs. No model was free of violations. The four best models violated in 22 to 24% of their runs. Yet one of them, Nova Pro, did the task correctly in only 30 runs.

documents.abstract: Gamified e-learning platforms and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven adaptive learning systems can improve learner engagement, but existing solutions rarely combine the two, and few explain their adaptive decisions to learners. To address this gap, we propose LearnSpace, a hybrid AI–gamification framework for responsive e-learning that adds an Explanation Layer, based on Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), to a deterministic reward architecture. The framework merges classical gamification mechanics with an AI personalization module in which experience points, rewards, and difficulty adjustments follow explicit weighted formulas. A Thompson-sampling bandit learns which feedback works best after a mistake. For each adaptive decision, the Explanation Layer names only the factors that drive it and turns them into a short justification for the learner. The design draws on a qualitative overview of 14 platforms, and the LearnSpace mobile prototype implements the gamification components and the bandit. In a pre-registered simulation with 500 synthetic learners per run, the first explanation rule named a factor that had no effect on the decision in 95.3% of difficulty adjustments, while the decision-specific rule never did. The bandit had lower regret than uniformly random feedback allocation. Effects on real learners remain to be tested.

documents.abstract: The security of Critical Infrastructures (CIs) is paramount, yet human operators frequently face cognitive overload when managing complex cyber-physical threats. This chapter presents a comprehensive overview of AVATAR4BC, a novel, personalized Intelligent Virtual Assistant (IVA) designed to address this critical human-factors challenge. Our system represents a paradigm shift from traditional dashboards by providing an embodied, conversational interface that leverages a high-fidelity 3D human avatar. A core contribution of AVATAR4BC is its multidisciplinary approach, which goes beyond technical integration. It fuses advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) with insights from the Social Sciences and Humanities (SSH). The system’s backend integrates Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Text-to-Speech (TTS), and real-time speech-driven facial animation to create a natural interaction. Crucially, it incorporates Explainable AI (XAI) principles by using Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate human-readable explanations of opaque Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) agent decisions from the underlying DYNABIC framework. Furthermore, AVATAR4BC’s personalization engine, informed by psychological and behavioral research, dynamically adapts the avatar’s appearance, voice, and communication style to the operator, aiming to reduce stress and enhance decision-making effectiveness. Final validation through end-to-end unit testing demonstrates the system’s core functionality, confirming the seamless integration of its architectural components. This work establishes a robust foundation for future research into human–AI collaboration, with significant implications for enhancing resilience in cybersecurity and other high-stakes domains.

documents.abstract: The growing need to strengthen decision making and sustainable performance in construction companies was examined in response to increasing complexity, competitive pressure, and technological transformation. The objective was to analyze the scientific evolution and main contributions of artificial intelligence as a strategic tool applied to business management in the construction sector. A systematic literature review was conducted using a bibliometric approach, an inductive method, and a mixed perspective through the identification, selection, analysis, and triangulation of studies published in academic databases. The results showed that artificial intelligence evolved from operational applications into a strategic organizational capability, particularly when integrated with digital ecosystems focused on information analysis, automation, and prediction. Relevant contributions were identified in planning, risk management, cost control, productivity, energy efficiency, occupational safety, and the reduction of environmental impacts. It was also found that the benefits achieved were conditioned by leadership, digital culture, technological maturity, data quality, interoperability, and specialized competencies. As a novel contribution, complementary theoretical perspectives were integrated to understand artificial intelligence as a strategic sociotechnical capability linked to the creation of sustainable competitive advantages. It was concluded that its adoption strengthened anticipatory capacity, decision quality, and economic, social, and environmental performance, although gaps persisted regarding empirical evidence, regulation, technological governance, and application in Latin American construction companies. Future research was recommended to validate these findings contextually and develop integrative models that could be applied at the organizational level. This synthesis highlighted the strategic interaction between technology, people, processes, organizational capabilities, and sustainability within contemporary construction management.

It examines how AI-based tools can support language learning, including improving learning efficiency, providing personalized learning experiences, and helping students practise English. The study also considers potential limitations and challenges associated with AI use in education. The purpose of this research is to examine the role of artificial intelligence in English language education and consider how it can be used effectively in the learning process. The project was conducted by a Grade 10 student as part of a school research project in the field of Humanities, within the section of Linguistics (English Language).

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming healthcare delivery, yet AI education specific to family medicine remains limited. Primary care physicians manage a uniquely diverse and often undifferentiated patient caseload; in this context, AI offers significant potential to enhance clinical decision-making, support administrative workflows, and strengthen the doctor-patient relationship — but only when paired with adequate training, safety assessment, and governance frameworks. Without robust training, AI adoption can introduce biases, lead to over-reliance on algorithmic recommendations, and compromise patient safety. Several competency frameworks for AI in medical education have been proposed at undergraduate and postgraduate levels, covering domains such as foundational knowledge, critical appraisal, ethical awareness, and clinical application. However, a significant gap persists in aligning AI education with the unique competencies of family medicine, including continuity, comprehensiveness, and patient-centredness. The World Organization of Family Doctors (WONCA) Europe definition of general practice provides a well-established competency framework that can guide this integration. This scoping review was conducted following the Arksey and O'Malley framework and reported according to the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. Five electronic databases were searched (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, EMBASE, and ERIC) for English-language publications from January 2000 to December 2024. Fifty-eight studies met the final inclusion criteria. The review pursues two complementary aims. First, it maps the existing literature on AI education in medical curricula to the six WONCA core competency domains (Primary Care Management, Person-Centred Care, Specific Problem-Solving Skills, Comprehensive Approach, Community Orientation, and Holistic Modeling). Second, it synthesises the curriculum frameworks proposed within the included studies to identify foundational AI competencies that transcend individual WONCA domains, such as AI and data science literacy, critical appraisal of AI outputs, ethics and privacy governance, prompt engineering, and continuous learning. The expected outcome is a dual-pillar curriculum framework comprising domain-specific WONCA-aligned AI competencies and cross-cutting foundational AI competencies, offering a structured, evidence-informed basis for integrating AI education into family medicine residency programmes. The review is being prepared for submission to Medical Teacher (Taylor & Francis).

documents.abstract: Mathematics education is being reshaped by artificial intelligence tools, which tailor instruction to individual learners through adaptive guidance and instant feedback, and in doing so can deepen conceptual understanding and build problem-solving capacity. Whether students accept such tools and keep using them, however, rests on a combination of cognitive, behavioral, and psychological conditions. The present study investigated how first-year female undergraduate students (N = 125) at a university in Saudi Arabia accept AI tools, and how psychologically resilient they are, within a mathematics learning environment supported by AI. A further aim was to determine how psychological resilience relates to both technology acceptance and learning engagement in that environment. A model was therefore constructed integrating the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), learning engagement, and psychological resilience. Data was gathered through a quantitative cross-sectional survey at the end of the semester and analyzed using descriptive statistics and Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). Participants reported high technology acceptance and psychological resilience. Model fit was satisfactory, and the proposed hypotheses were supported. Psychological resilience was positively associated with both technology acceptance and learning engagement, and was indirectly associated with behavioral intention through the model’s mediating constructs, of which perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use are the first links. By adding psychological resilience and learning engagement to TAM, these findings may broaden the model and help clarify how these constructs relate to AI acceptance in AI-supported mathematics learning.

documents.abstract: Biomarkers are measurable biological characteristics that can support disease diagnosis, prognosis, treatment selection, and monitoring oftherapeutic response. Their discovery increasingly depends on high-dimensional and heterogeneous data such as genomics, transcriptomics,proteomics, medical imaging, electronic health records, and wearable-device measurements. Artificial intelligence (AI) can help identifypatterns across these sources and support more efficient clinical-trial planning, including patient stratification, eligibility screening, recruitmentforecasting, endpoint assessment, and risk monitoring. This paper presents a conceptual framework connecting AI-enabled biomarker discoverywith clinical-trial optimization. The framework covers data governance, preprocessing, multimodal feature integration, candidate selection,validation, trial feasibility, and continuous monitoring. It emphasizes that computational performance alone does not establish clinicalusefulness: candidate biomarkers require independent replication, analytical validation, clinical validation, and evidence of utility in a clearlydefined context of use. The paper synthesizes published literature and regulatory principles; it does not report a newly conducted clinical studyor claim original performance results. Responsible implementation requires privacy protection, representative data, transparent documentation,clinician oversight, and prospective evaluation before AI outputs influence patient care.

The current study, which is entitled Evaluating the Assessing the Acceptance of ChatGPT Among Higher Education Students: A Case Study in Pahang, aimed to assess the behavioural intention of university students with regard to using ChatGPT in various academic levels. The Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2) was selected as a cross-sectional survey approach, data were collected from 184 respondents between March and May 2025 through both online and printed questionnaires. The core antecedents included in the analysis were the performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, hedonic motivation, habit, and personal innovativeness and were operationalised using a five-point Likert scale. Descriptive analysis revealed an overall mean behavioural intention score of 3.523 (SD = 0.901), indicating a generally positive inclination toward ChatGPT adoption. Notably, both bachelor and postgraduate students erred higher mean scores (4.400 and 4.370, respectively) in comparison with students of the foundation level (3.393), which suggests that students of higher learning level assign AI-based technologies a higher academic rating. These results highlight an increasing openness to generative AI among the population of higher education, and at the same time, they indicate the presence of strong inequalities among the academic layers. Therefore, the findings reinforce the need to introduce specific AI-literacy programmes and responsible digital education to facilitate fair and responsible usage. Despite the methodological constraints, such as sampling, and the disproportional number of groups, the generalisability of the findings is diluted but still, the study provides useful information to the growing discourse on AI implementation into higher education, at least in the developing regional milieus. Moreover, the study presents practical research implications to institutions of higher education working to come up with evidence-based, inclusionary, and ethically sustainable strategies to implement ChatGPT and other similar technologies in pedagogical and curricular contexts.

Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming quality assurance in higher education by enabling adaptive, data-driven assessments of teaching performance and student learning. This integrative review synthesizes the purposes, methodologies, and outcomes of AI-enabled assessments, examines emerging technological trends, and identifies opportunities for improving teaching quality and learner support. Methods An integrative review was conducted using the Whittemore and Knafl framework, with study identification and selection reported in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Of 367 records identified, 21 studies were included. Methodological quality was appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Descriptive and thematic analyses were supplemented by keyword network mapping using VOSviewer version 1.6.20. Results Most studies were multi-authored (71.43%) and published in interdisciplinary education and technology journals (57.14%), with publication activity concentrated in 2024 (28.57%) and 2025 (33.33%). The Western Pacific Region accounted for the largest proportion of studies (38.10%), while no studies originated from the African Region. Teacher performance was the predominant assessment focus ( n = 11; 52.38%), followed by learner behavior ( n = 4; 19.05%) and learner performance ( n = 3; 14.29%). Teacher-focused assessments primarily analyzed learner-generated data using machine learning and natural language processing, whereas some learner-focused assessments employed video-based data and computer vision. Machine learning and natural language processing were the most frequently identified technological approaches ( n = 6), followed by computer vision and multimodal or speech recognition approaches ( n = 3). Most implementations followed a data-input, AI-processing, and output-generation structure, with varying levels of complexity. Thematic analysis identified four domains, while keyword network analysis revealed eight clusters. Discussion The findings highlight a fragmented assessment landscape in which teacher performance and learner behavior are predominantly examined independently. Although learner behavior may provide complementary evidence of teaching effectiveness, reciprocal relationships between teaching and learning remain insufficiently explored. Geographic disparities and methodological heterogeneity further constrain the generalizability and institutional applicability of existing evidence. Conclusion AI offers promising opportunities to strengthen teaching evaluation and learner support in higher education. However, broader geographic representation, methodological rigor, validated assessment frameworks, and equitable, human-supervised implementation are essential to ensure that institutional adoption is guided by robust evidence. Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as cognitive interfaces that shape how users interpret evidence, communicate, and make decisions. As deployed systems become more multimodal, tool-using, and multi-agent, safety failures no longer arise only from isolated harmful outputs, but also from how agents update, store, and propagate epistemic commitments across retrieval, memory, tools, and peer communication. In this paper, we define belief as an engineering abstraction for evidence-based commitments that guide downstream action. Building on this view, we propose the Explicit Belief Multi-Agent System (EB-MAS), which externalizes belief states into a structured substrate, uses belief operators to propose candidate updates, and applies a Cognitive Firewall to bound or reject updates that are weakly evidenced but strongly driven by vulnerability cues. We also discuss the risk of group belief at the group level, including manufactured consensus, collusion, and cascading misinformation, and outline practical integration challenges around grounding, false positives, scalability, and ethical misuse. Therefore, scalable agent safety requires not only better output filtering or stronger base models, but also explicit interfaces for tracing, calibrating, and constraining belief revision at runtime.

Generative AI now produces images and poems that people cannot reliably distinguish from human-made work, so people often judge for themselves who made a work. We examine how these perceived-authorship judgments relate to aesthetic preference. In a public online AI Art Turing Test, 11,123 people judged whether each of 50 pictures (26 AI-generated) was made by a human and were asked for their favourite. Among the 9,152 respondents who judged their favourite, a picture was 22.1 percentage points more likely to be judged human-made when it was the respondent's favourite, holding respondent and picture fixed. The association was similar for AI-generated and human-made favourites, was positive for all 50 pictures, and appeared under every reported detection strategy. Respondents most negative about AI art chose fewer AI-generated favourites (47% against 60% among the most positive) but more often believed them human-made, partly because others also judged those pictures human. As a result, in every opinion group a third to two fifths of respondents named an AI-generated favourite they believed human-made. A reanalysis of a published experiment on AI-generated poetry, in which 230 people rated each poem before judging its authorship, found the same pattern, although the AI poems were rated higher. When provenance is hidden, liking and perceived human authorship travel together, consistent with aesthetic response serving as evidence of a human maker and with beliefs about the maker shaping enjoyment. The findings qualify research on bias against AI art, which typically uses explicit labels, and inform AI disclosure policy.

Abstract Introduction Medical Artificial Intelligence (MAI) is transforming healthcare but raises significant ethical concerns. Despite emerging principles and regulations, to our knowledge, no standardized clinical bioethics framework exists to guide MAI practice. Objective This Delphi study sought global expert agreement on ethical challenges, principles, guidelines, and practical tools for MAI use. Method A four-round international eDelphi study, conducted under ACCORD and DELPHISTAR guidance, engaged multidisciplinary stakeholders identified through systematic review and targeted recruitment. Preliminary items were evidence-derived and iteratively refined. Consensus (≥ 80% agreement across two rounds) was predefined. Surveys were anonymized and randomized. Ethical approval and protocol registration were secured before study initiation. Results The panel included 53 participants from 21 countries. Survey rounds started November 2025 and ended February 2026. 170 items were considered. 132 reached consensus. Items were classified into bioethical issues, values, principles, solutions, a checklist for clinicians, and report markers for risk management. Discussion This study produced clinician-focused practice guidelines for the bioethical use of MAI. Ethical components aligned with prior literature, while no new bioethical principles met consensus. Limitations included geographic imbalance and stakeholder representation. Recommendations emphasized human responsibility, governance, and practical implementation tools. Conclusion This Delphi consensus provides practical, ethics-based guidance for the responsible integration of MAI into clinical practice and institutional governance.

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in clinical reasoning, documentation, prediction, communication, and delegated digital and physical action via agentic and embodied systems. The central ethical challenge is no longer limited to identifying which tasks AI can automate, but determining which human competencies become essential as technological capabilities expand. Methods: This concept paper employs a five-step analysis: technological horizon mapping, selective synthesis of work-transformation evidence, conceptual analysis of medical action, normative synthesis, and medico-legal interpretation. Results: We propose a four-domain framework addressing four core questions of responsible medical action: epistemic (What is true?), normative (What ought to be done?), anthropological–relational (Who is the subject of care?), and systemic–hermeneutic (What does this mean here and now?). Grounded in a conception of technology as augmentative alteration, the framework recognises that technological capabilities can enhance beneficial action but also amplify harm; technological capability alone therefore cannot determine its appropriate use. We also distinguish interpersonal relationships from clinical human–machine interaction, propose professional exigibility as an analytical medico-legal category, and argue that meaningful human oversight requires more than mere human presence. Conclusions: The findings outline key implications for clinical practice, medical education, healthcare organizations, regulation, and a future empirical research agenda focused on human–AI error convergence.

This independent white paper explores how artificial intelligence could reshape procurement beyond the automation of established processes and conventional human-in-the-loop approval models. Drawing on procurement leadership experience, ecosystem thinking, human–AI collaboration and research into organisational learning, it proposes cognitive orchestration as an operating philosophy through which machine intelligence, automation and professional expertise interact across an extended enterprise. Central to the argument is the distinction between continuous human judgement and constant human intervention. The paper proposes that human agency, ethical responsibility and contextual understanding should shape intelligent systems throughout their operation, while dependable activities are automated wherever appropriate. It also introduces reciprocal intelligence and regenerative value as complementary concepts, considering how AI-enabled procurement might improve decision-making, strengthen relationships and develop organisational capability rather than focus exclusively on efficiency. A deployed spend-intelligence model provides an example of adaptive human engagement in practice. The wider ecosystem framework is presented as a conceptual proposition for further investigation, not as an empirically validated operating model.

Digital mental health is often framed as a problem of access that technology can solve through scalability, personalization, and continuous monitoring. Yet the expansion of apps, telepsychology, passive sensing, and generative artificial intelligence also transforms what counts as psychological knowledge, how distress is interpreted, and who assumes responsibility for care. This essay advances a relational–ecological account of digital mental health grounded in five propositions: psychological distress cannot be reduced to computational signals; digital access is not equivalent to meaningful care; personalization without contextual justice can intensify inequity; privacy and informed refusal are therapeutic conditions rather than merely regulatory constraints; and successful innovation must preserve human agency and accountable therapeutic relationships. Drawing on intervention research, implementation science, digital phenotyping, critical data studies, and minority-stress perspectives, the essay proposes the CARE framework—Context, Agency, Relationships, and Equity—as a normative evaluative heuristic for design, evaluation, and governance that complements existing app-evaluation and implementation frameworks. Privacy and informed refusal are treated as components of Agency, each domain is paired with indicators and illustrative failure conditions, and the framework is applied to three archetypal technologies. Rather than reject digital technologies, the argument identifies the conditions under which they can extend psychological care without reproducing surveillance, exclusion, or technological solutionism. Future research should test the six propositions derived from the framework and foreground clinically meaningful outcomes, subgroup validity, longitudinal harms, hybrid care pathways, and participatory governance.

Teachers work in socially and emotionally complex environments that require rapid professional decision making under conditions of uncertainty. Classroom simulations provide opportunities for preservice and in-service teachers to practice, receive feedback, and reflect without placing students or teachers at unnecessary risk. Despite their growing use, the field lacks a contemporary and inclusive definition of classroom simulation. Existing frameworks often categorize simulations by technology or immersion level, overlooking important differences in agency, responsiveness, adaptation, and instructional design. These limitations have become more significant with the emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) and AI agents. This conceptual paper defines classroom simulations as deliberately designed approximations of classroom practice embedded within a structured learning process that includes preparation, enactment, and reflection. We propose a four-layer framework encompassing the professional practice represented, the simulated situation, the distribution of agency and adaptation, and the orchestration of learning. The framework is used to examine how simulations can support social-emotional and inclusive teaching competencies and how AI may influence scenario generation, student behaviour enactment, personalization, and feedback. Effective implementation requires theoretically grounded representations of learners and classroom interactions, alignment with learning goals, meaningful human oversight, and protections for agency, inclusion, privacy, and emotional safety.

documents.abstract: Introduction – Objectives Global mental health increasingly requires approaches that address psychological well-being within biological, social, cultural, and technological contexts. Contemporary mental-health systems often prioritize individual symptoms and clinical interventions, while culturally embedded understandings of health, family relationships, social belonging, and meaning may receive less attention. Drawing on Traditional Chinese mind–body perspectives, this study proposes a collaborative mental-health framework that integrates culturally grounded health concepts, community and family participation, and emerging artificial intelligence (AI) technologies within existing public-health and healthcare systems. The objective is to develop a human-centred model that supports psychological well-being, social functioning, and health equity while maintaining scientific and clinical standards. Methodology The proposed framework was developed through conceptual synthesis of Traditional Chinese mind–body theory, family and relational perspectives on well-being, community mental-health promotion, and emerging approaches to AI-enabled healthcare. Rather than treating traditional concepts as substitutes for clinical diagnosis or evidence-based treatment, the framework considers their potential contribution to culturally responsive health communication, prevention, health education, and community engagement. It identifies complementary roles for healthcare professionals, public-health agencies, families, community organizations, researchers, and technology developers in supporting psychological well-being across different stages of life. Results and Discussion The framework identifies three interconnected dimensions of collaborative mental-health promotion: mind–body integration, relational support, and technological augmentation. Traditional concepts concerning the relationship among xin (心), yi (意), and shi (識) provide a culturally meaningful vocabulary for discussing attention, emotional experience, self-understanding, and well-being, while family and community relationships provide social contexts for psychological support and restoration of social functioning. AI technologies may complement these approaches through health education, personalized information, early identification of psychosocial needs, and coordination of community resources, provided that appropriate safeguards for privacy, autonomy, equity, and human oversight are maintained. The framework therefore positions AI not as a replacement for clinicians or communities, but as a tool supporting collaborative and human-centred care. Conclusions A sustainable global mental-health architecture should accommodate diverse cultural understandings of well-being while remaining grounded in scientific evidence, clinical responsibility, and human rights. Integrating Traditional Chinese mind–body perspectives, family and community participation, and responsibly governed AI offers a potential model for more culturally responsive and participatory mental-health promotion. By connecting healthcare, families, communities, public authorities, and technology developers, the framework seeks to strengthen psychological resilience, preserve social participation across the life course, and contribute to more equitable and humane health systems.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) assignments are spreading rapidly in business and technology higher education, yet published accounts rarely report whether every student can take part on fair terms. This systematic review audited published GenAI assignments against the social, economic, institutional and environmental dimensions of pedagogical sustainability. Following PRISMA 2020, OpenAlex (2023–2026) was searched, 1092 peer-reviewed records were screened and 191 studies were included. Each assignment was coded for its creative family, access and fairness provisions, ethics content and assessment, and scored on a 0–5 inclusion-readiness index. An AI system served as primary coder; a human coder double-coded 30 studies and the author adjudicated all disagreements. Most assignments used GenAI as a tutor or thinking partner (52%). Provisions were scarce: 27% ensured free access, 2% offered a non-AI alternative task and 2% addressed disability. Privacy (53%) and opt-out (35%) appeared mainly as research-ethics safeguards rather than design features. Mean inclusion readiness was 1.30 of 5 (0.75 on design-only coding). Only one study in seven taught GenAI ethics, and environmental cost was taught once. Business courses favored choice and language support; technology courses favored central access. The index offers a measurable design and reporting checklist for sustainable GenAI pedagogy.
